body:
## Module 4 in two minutes

The most frequent thing you write, and the thing most likely to be read years later by somebody whose job is to undermine it. So the question isn't *how do I use AI on this document* — it's **what does the document have to do**, and the AI permissions follow from that.

**Six elements a finder of fact looks for.** What was alleged, each allegation separately, in the complainant's terms. What was investigated — and **what was excluded and why.** What evidence was gathered and from whom, including what was sought and not obtained. **What could not be established, and why** — the element most templates omit entirely. What was found, allegation by allegation. And on what standard, named and applied visibly.

> **A report organized as a narrative is a report whose gaps are invisible. A report organized as elements makes its own gaps visible to you first.**

A gap in a narrative reads as a transition — *"following the meeting, the complainant raised further concerns…"*; did you investigate the meeting? Prose carries the reader past the joint, including when the reader is you re-reading your own draft. A gap in an elements report is a blank space with a heading over it.

And the structure sets the permissions: **elements one to four are rungs one and two, where AI is permitted and useful. Elements five and six are rungs four and five. Nothing.**

### Which allegation did I fail to resolve?

The generalist completeness question is *what did I fail to ask?* Good question, wrong defect. **The specialist version catches the one that ends investigations.**

A complainant raises four things. Three are substantial; one is vague, or awkward, or arrived in a final paragraph. The investigation addresses three. **The fourth is never mentioned again** — not rejected, not found unsubstantiated, not recorded as outside scope. It just disappears.

Why that specific defect is so damaging: **it's mechanical to detect**, so opposing counsel finds it first and free. **It's unanswerable** — you cannot explain why allegation four wasn't addressed if nobody made a decision about it. And **it's frequently the one that mattered**, because the vague final-paragraph allegation is often the protected-characteristic or retaliation complaint, which arrives last and least clearly precisely because it's hardest to say.

**And it's a genuinely good use of AI**, which is why it's here rather than in a warning. It's a coverage audit against a list: allegations in, findings out, flag the mismatches. It evaluates nobody. Rung two, fully permitted, and a model doesn't get bored at item four.

Two rules that make it work. **"Outside scope" and "insufficient evidence to determine" are resolutions. Silence is not.** And run it against **the complainant's own framing** — restating an allegation more narrowly and resolving the narrower version is the same defect wearing a suit.

**The full module applies the ladder at sentence level**, which is where it either works or turns out to have been a diagram. Three sentences, same length, same tense: *"Raised his voice twice, according to two witnesses"* is an observation. *"Was hostile during the meeting"* is a **finding wearing an observation's grammar** — nobody said "hostile"; you concluded it. *"Intended to intimidate"* is a **determination smuggled into a clause.** The last two aren't lies and may be right. The problem is that the sentence gives a reader no way to tell which rung produced it.

So: **a model may tell you a sentence has climbed a rung. It may never tell you which rung is right.** Flagging is a linguistic audit you can check in seconds. Choosing is the finding. Which means *"identify sentences containing characterizations or conclusions and quote them"* is fine, and *"rewrite these neutrally"* is not — that hands the model the choice of what the neutral version asserts.

**And privilege, which now has case law pointing both ways** `[V]`. In February 2026 an SDNY judge held material generated through a **consumer AI tool** at a party's own prompting was not privileged — inputting it was sharing with a third party, and *Kovel* didn't apply partly because the party engaged the tool **on their own initiative rather than at counsel's direction.** In May 2026, in *Mobley*, bias-testing data **was** protected, because attorneys curated the analysis and used it in legal advice.

**Two rulings, opposite outcomes, and the variable was whether counsel directed the work.** Neither is a workplace-investigation holding. The practical move is cheap: **if a matter may be privileged, the AI question belongs in the engagement, not afterwards.**
